video_title: Why Global Bond Yields Are Surging
transcript: Bond yields around the world have been rising for  most of this year and have recently surged. So are   interest rates settling into a new higher normal  or is this a temporary dislocation? I'm Allison   Nathan and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges to  understand why bond markets are under pressure   giving rise to higher bond yields. I'm sitting  down with my colleague George Cole who leads   European rate strategy for Goldman Sachs Research.  George joins me today from London. George, welcome   to the program. Thanks very much. So George, it's  easy to look at the headlines and think this is   just a US story. We've obviously seen concern  about inflation here in the US. There's concern   about spending levels, but this bond selloff is  really happening everywhere. Is that right? Yeah.   No, that's right. So, as you said, I sit over  here in London. I look primarily at the European   uh bond markets uh in Germany, in the UK. uh  but when we look at the US, when we look at   markets like Japan, we would really think of these  four as the as the major government bond markets   uh the the the major benchmarks for the for the  global economy and global fixed income markets.   And we're seeing all of these markets move higher  in yield. We're at multi-deade highs as we,   you know, read about in the financial press.  We're seeing yields pressing higher across all   of these economies. And it doesn't look obvious  that there's a single driver or a single market   that is really leading the sell-off or or driving  it over a long period of time. From day to day,   one move might be bigger in one of those  economies, but really over the last few months,   all of those markets have been pushing yields  higher. Well, well, that's my follow-up to you,   George, because the question is what is driving  this? And and and my intuition would be the rest   of the world is just following the US lead, but  you're saying that that may not be the case. every   country might be dealing with their own issues.  Yeah. So, as a as a rate strategist and as an   economist, we'd be looking at yield curves and and  bond markets to try to, you know, think about and   and find clues what is what is driving the move.  We could look which economy might be driving it.   Uh, as I said, you know, it's not that obvious  that you can point to just one of those major   bond markets as driving the selloff. uh you could  look at things like the shape of the yield curve.   Maybe it's the front end of interest rate curves  that is moving. That would be associated with   expectations around policy rates that might be on  the move. Maybe reflecting cyclical conditions,   better growth, higher inflation. It could be  maybe the long end of the curve is moving. That   could be a term premier type of type of issue.  the price of duration risk, maybe fiscal risks,   or maybe even long-term growth further out the  curve. And what we're seeing across the yield   curve is that all the way from the 30-year point  on the curve, which has got a lot of attention,   and yields are much higher there than they  have been in recent decades, but all the way   down the 10-year point on the curve and even  the policy rate expectations or pricing uh one   or two years out is looking much higher. Maybe  not right at the peak of where we were in 2022,   but certainly very high relative to where we've  been in recent years. So it looks like we've got   broadbased pressure across a range of different  factors. And so what are then the the fundamental   drivers or are there not? I mean, what do you  attribute all of this movement to? I'm glad you   you you asked. Are there fundamentals behind it?  And this is one of the features of this sell-off I   think is a little underappreciated when you uh you  know when you might read about it is that actually   the volatility of the moves have been relatively  low. Now of course we're dealing with the revision   right now of central bank expectations and we're  maybe moving toward an expectation that rates will   be moving higher from central banks. That's now  inducing a little bit of volatility in the market.   But if we go back to say July and think about  the move since then in yields higher, what has   been really striking is that volatility has been  low v both the realized volatility of the market   and also the price of volatility the implied  volatility that is priced into the market as well.   Now, we might be a little bit higher in the range  of the year, but if you look at on a multi-year   horizon, volatility is actually quite low. And  that feature of this sell-off makes it much   harder to argue, well, this is a non-funddamental  move. This is happening because of some sort of   technical reason or uh a move in the market that  has outsized volatility that is not sustainable.   When volatility remains low, it is harder to make  that conclusion. What I would say is that there   is an overlapping set of fundamentals here that  are driving yields up and that goes all the way   from longunning themes like large deficits,  fiscal policy that is driving debt levels to   uh you know to historic or or recent highs. We've  had that since the pandemic. Now that's not always   and everywhere a guide to what markets do. uh  but when you combine that with something that is   operating over the last few years uh the borrowing  associated with AI capex as more and more of   the AI capex is financed in debt markets uh we  are seeing there's some competition now uh for   government borrowing and then the final layer this  year we've actually had pretty resilient growth   across major economies and very locally and this  is driving some of the most recent volatility we   are seeing a renewed push higher in energy prices  uh following the ongoing war in Iran. That is   uh the last kind of inflationary uh push that is  worrying the market. Now what those things are   combining to do, we know we've got this backdrop  of elevated government supply. We've now got   competition from private sector issuance just at  the moment that bond demand is weaker because of   higher inflation and actually resilient growth in  the economy and all of those things combined we   think fundamentally to push yields up. Right.  But when I look at those list of factors the   most recent one of course has been the surge in  energy prices and so my question is why now when   many of those factors have been sort of long in  the market long in coming? Is that your answer?   energy or it's still a question we're trying  to answer. I I think that this is exactly the   you know the the the move very recently. So if  we think about uh the the potential for Bank   of England rate hikes or further ECB rate hikes,  the potential for the Fed to hike, those things   are more uh determined by the the nearer term  inflation considerations, particularly in Europe,   where we've got not only rising uh oil prices,  but also European gas prices. This is creating   a real headache uh for the inflation outlook in  Europe. There's no doubt the surge from energy   prices should prove temporary, but it feels like  the central banks there now are running out of   a bit of patience uh to deal with what should  be temporary shocks and are willing to take a   little bit more action to safeguard inflation  further down the line. So you're right that is   what is driving the latest round of interest rate  movements and they have been a bit more volatile   and certainly when the central bank comes into  play that is when you do see a little bit more   of a pickup in rates volatility but that really  hasn't been the story of the entire sell-off not   say if we rewind to something like July the move  has been more gradual more orderly and driven by   the long end of the curve which suggests some  of these more longer running factors that you   mentioned also are contributing but I I would  certainly stress that it is the overlap and   combination of these factors that I think gets  us to where we are today. So the other major   development uh in the recent period has been that  the US Treasury has been engaged in bond buybacks.   Tell us more about that and its implications. Why  are they doing that? Yeah, so the bond buybacks is   a program that the US Treasury uh have had for for  some years now. Uh the idea of the of the program   is to uh if you think about the bond market, the  most liquid bonds that are out there in the system   are the ones that have been issued recently. The  bonds that have been issued some time ago have   uh you know are less liquid. There's less turnover  in these bonds. And so the buyback program is   designed to take some of those less liquid bonds  out of the system and replace them with fresher   bonds. So if you think about that motivation, it's  kind of a liquidity operation. It just greases the   bond market with these newer, fresher, fresher  bonds. The announcement uh some weeks ago uh   that we heard from the US Treasury would that be  that they would increase the size of buybacks at   the long end of the curve and the practical effect  of that will be to reduce the maturity of the debt   stock. you would be taking out uh some of these  less liquid bonds maybe over over a a 10 or 20 or   30-year maturity and you would be replacing them  with bonds that you're issuing usually uh at lower   maturities and maybe even using treasury bills.  And so in effect this is a switch to take um uh uh   longer maturity but less liquid bonds out of the  system and replace them with uh shorter maturity   bonds. If we think about that in the context of  what other treasuries across the major economies,   so the UK debt management office, the DMO is a  good example of this. At the end of last year,   the DMO announced that they would be reducing the  amount of 30-year bonds that they would be issuing   to the market. And that did have some effect to  lower the yield in the 30-year part of the curve,   but only on a relative basis. Little bit of a  curve effect and a little bit of an effect to   support 30-year yields lower against say swap  rates. What it didn't do was change the macro   price of the bond or the level of the yields.  Only really the fundamentals, expectations   around policy, around uh fiscal policy, around  uh inflation can do that. And again, the UK is a   great example here. Despite the fact we haven't  seen very many 30-year bonds issued recently,   uh 30-year yields are still near the highs. And  so, in that sense, it's not going to change the   macro fundamentals, right, George? But I do think  the market interpretation of this announcement,   which I think was somewhat unexpected, please  correct me if I'm wrong, was that this was an   attempt by the Treasury to reduce long yields.  But you don't think it will have that effect,   setting their motivations aside. That's not  your observation. Yeah. So I think that the   the announcement came uh in an unanticipated  way. it was not in the regular schedule of the   uh you know the communication of the US Treasury  to the market via its refunding announcements and   so in that sense there was initially a bit of  ambiguity about exactly you know what what the   program was designed to achieve. uh you know part  of the uh rationale subsequently was that there w   would be some attempt to improve liquidity at  the long end of the curve and again following   the pattern that we're seeing in the other debt  management offices or the other treasuries and   issuers across sovereign markets it does seem a  very natural thing to try to balance the supply   and demand dynamics across the yield curve  there are deficits to finance and the Treasury   in the US and elsewhere need to make a decision.  How do we finance that? What's the optimal way   to issue that debt? Well, when we have a situation  where yields are high, central banks are no longer   buying debt, we've got reduced demand for from say  pension funds, other uh investors that typically   buy these longerdated bonds. there's lower  demand because at these higher yield levels   liabilities of say uh pension systems that uh  are being discounted at these higher levels of   rates they are now much lower and so that demand  has actually fallen despite the fact yields have   moved higher and that means that treasuries and  issuers it makes a lot of sense to think about   lowering the amount of long longerdated issuance  uh and and relying on more liquid and and lower   and shorter maturities and that's exactly what  we've seen across a number of economies. So as   long as you know that that if we view that as  the as the pattern that we're seeing across these   sovereign issuers then this increased buybacks at  the long end is just a different way to do that.   You could reduce auction sizes or you could do  these buybacks to get these longerdated bonds out   of the market. In the end that the effect will  be the same. But I I certainly would would uh   would say the evidence across whether it's the  UK that I mentioned, Japan to some extent has   made some steps to reduce long issuance. That's  not really doing much to change the macro price.   Uh and we are seeing yields in those markets very  much being determined by the deeper fundamentals.   Are there worries about inflation or fiscal risks?  Are there issuance pressures that are you know um   maybe outside of governments that are also leading  to those higher yields? Those are the things that   are really going to determine the level of yields.  Understood. Let's get back again to some of these   drivers of these long-term bond yields, uh, you  know, reaching higher levels. We we've talked   about the US dealing with really an unprecedented  deficit outside of wartimes, but there's also   rising regional tensions that are forcing Europe  and Asia to spend heavily on their own defense.   So, we are seeing sort of fiscal pressures  globally. Does that really mean again just   coming back to the drivers that higher rates are  just really simply the cost or maybe the permanent   cost of today's fiscal and to some extent even  geopolitical realities. Yeah. So I think that when   when we be looking at the fiscal outlook, what you  what you really want to be paying attention to,   uh what have what are the non-discretionary  elements of the budget spending uh that are that   are committed to uh entitlement spending obviously  a big one and and has importance across all of   the major economies and interest costs. And this  is something as we keep rolling over government   debt at these higher levels of yields, this is a  non-negotiable cost that governments need to pay.   So there is pressure on budgets from that source.  And if you add on that commitments to increase   defense spending uh which as you mentioned  across a number of geographies but certainly   here in Europe that is a that is a commitment  that you're increasingly seeing uh governments   make. The UK being a great example of that. It  does lead to very challenging budget choices. You   need to think how will that additional spending be  financed when the budget's already under pressure.   It could be via higher revenue, higher taxation.  It could be via reduced spending elsewhere. Or it   could be by renewed borrowing. And so that's why  the bond market is is watching uh fiscal events   and wants to understand exactly what priorities  governments will be giving. Of course, we're   also in a situation where there is a competition  for savings. And I mentioned before, we've got a   situation where the private sector is undertaking  a very significant uplift of capex. Borrowing is   being used to finance that. And so just at the  moment where governments are attempting this   uplift in some areas of spending, there is now  a competition for savings. And if we think about   what that does to the savings investment balance  globally, we have fewer savings, we have more   investment. And the way to clear that market is  by raising interest rates. So it may not be here   forever, but uh it certainly is an environment  where at the moment while those spending pressures   or spending commitments are under pressure  to expand and there's a competition for those   global savings, we should expect that higher  rates uh you know are part of the environment,   right? Let's zoom out for a moment, George. I  mean I'm looking at the screen at you know over   5% 10year US yields. That seems so high to me.  But if we really think about history, that was   much closer to the, you know, pre global financial  crisis norm. So in some sense, is this really just   a return to a normal potentially even healthier  environment? Yeah. So I if you look at the long   uh sweep of, you know, the long time series  of yields, you're absolutely right. We're now,   you know, we haven't seen these levels for many  decades maybe in some in some cases, but if you   look at the longer history of yields, the levels  that we're at are not all that unusual and I think   consistent with some of the big shifts that we've  seen say over the last 5 years or so. The most   obvious one is the big shift higher in both the  level and the distribution of inflation risk.   uh that if you compare that to where we were in  the decade following the global financial crisis   into the pandemic couldn't be more different. That  was when we were worried about you know weakness   in demand very weak inflation outcomes. Policy  couldn't quite generate the inflation repress um   that uh that it wanted to and so the distribution  of risks in the bond market was to lower yields.   Now we have a distribution of inflation  outcomes that looks maybe even higher than   central bank targets if you know but certainly  much more symmetric around around central bank   targets and in in some sense that connects us  back to something looks a little more normal   um relative to uh the the decade following  the global financial crisis. There is one big   difference which is fiscal positions are different  to where they were uh back in a period where   yields were higher both nominal yields and real  yields. We now have much bigger debt burdens. We   have bigger deficits. So that is something that  you know is much more part of the discussion.   Can you have a normal yield environment this high  with fiscal policy as it is currently struck? Uh   one of the ways I think you can delay answering  that question is high nominal growth. as long   as growth both on the real side, but if you also  have a a cushion of inflation is higher, that is   something that can sustain yields at these levels.  But those are the questions for the future. How   will we bear the rise in interest costs that  the current yield curve would imply? And then   maybe when I think about some specific markets,  somewhere like Germany, the German uh yield curve   is not yet back to levels that we saw pre- global  financial crisis. There are good reasons for that.   I think as we learned through not only the GFC but  then the European sovereign crisis uh the rise of   credit spreads in European sovereign markets  does create a little bit of a more challenging   environment to sustain much higher bon yields. If  you have high bond yields plus a credit spread to   other sovereign markets in Europe, that creates  um you know much tighter financial conditions uh   for borrowing and some of those other economies.  And so there is something that is probably going   to keep the the distribution of German yields  a little lower. On the flip side of that,   we're seeing maybe now the prospect of something  like sustainable 2% or something close to it in   Japan uh in inflation. And that's something we  haven't seen for several decades. And so it does   look like Japanese yields might be at a higher  end of the range relative to they've uh you know   they've seen in in in recent decades, right?  But so if you think about the forward George,   what are you expecting in terms of rates? Will  they remain at these elevated levels? Where do   we go from here? Yeah. So going back to one of the  things we mentioned before, this selloff is broad.   It's been across the curve. It's been across  economies and although we are maybe now witnessing   something that looks a little bit more volatile as  central banks come into play generally it's been   a relatively low vol selloff that tells you that  there are probably fundamental views in the market   behind the selloff. So my view is it's going to  take a fundamental to beat a fundamental. And   so if you want to get yields lower, you've got to  have one of uh well some sort of pathway to lower   inflation I think is is the uh most obvious way  to think about um uh what would get yields lower.   uh the approximate source of that if you wanted  to see you know think about a reversal of what's   driving yields higher in the very short run is  uh global energy prices so both the oil market   uh refined products the European gas market that  is really difficult to have a lot of conviction   on in the near term given its link to uh the  geopolitical events the war in Iran um and and so   uh near-term visibility is really hard on a six  to 12 month basis our commodity strategist just   do expect at some point you know these commodity  markets are likely to be better supplied uh and   see those prices come down. So are we still  worried about energy price inflation in 6 to   12 months time? We hope not. We forecast not. That  would be one way to get lower yields particularly   in the front end of the curve where central banks  don't need to quite be as worried as maybe the   market thinks they will be uh about about the  energy price inflation. And then over the longer   run, I think an interesting one is to think about  what happens to this AI investment cycle. Uh and   at some point you would imagine that investment  needs will decrease once the investments begin to   bear fruit. And one of the questions for the  rates markets is can you seamlessly go from   the borrowing phase to the implementation phase  where you know we we transition into this world of   higher growth and higher productivity. That might  include a higher cost of capital further down the   line. But to the extent there's any bumps in that  journey, if investment expectations were to fall,   if there was some sort of other growth shock  that uh that could see a revision of some of   those expectations, uh if there's maybe some of  the disinflationary impacts of of AI productivity   growth that happen a little faster than expected,  that would be the other way that you could imagine   some of the pressure that we're seeing in the bond  market is alleviated. Um, and so in that sense,   those seem to me to be both in the near- term  and the more medium-term the most plausible   drivers. Of course, we'd be watching things like  fiscal policy very closely, and if you do see a   move toward uh fiscal tightening or something  changes in the fiscal trajectory, that would be   uh that would be also something as a as a as a  sign for lower yields. But as it stands, I think   near-term energy prices, that's what's delivering  a lot of the near-term uh movement and volatility   in markets. And then the forward trajectory of the  AI capex cycle is really the key thing to watch,   right? So still a lot of uncertainty of course  around all of those factors. So so what would be   your key takeaway, George, for investors right  now? Should they be re-evaluating the duration   of risk profiles within their portfolios um or  just see how this evolves and hold tight? Yeah,   in the very near term, the risk to bonds is coming  from the energy markets. And then I think most   importantly the connection to central bank pricing  where central banks they just run out of road they   you know can't tolerate the inflation anymore and  they need to hike. That would be the most you know   plausible approximate risk that would manifest  in the front end and that would be an environment   where uh the yield curve would flatten. In that  situation, you probably would see a decline in in   uh growth expectations, maybe inflation  expectations further out the curve. That wouldn't   necessarily see longerterm yields a lot higher.  You might see stability out in the forward curve.   And if we think about that then in combination  with the broader investment outlook where there   is whether it's the equity market or credit  markets you know a huge amount of connection to   the AI investment theme that is when you can maybe  start to build a portfolio where bonds have some   hedge value where if we find that that AI capex  trajectory you know undersshoots expectations   or that there is some sort of disinflationary  impact that comes comes faster than expected   and rates need to move lower. That is when  you can start to build a case that although   it's very uncertain what happens in the next  three months, maybe yields are a little higher,   certainly if we don't see any energy relief,  if you start to think about the distribution   of outcomes over a two, three, fouryear horizon,  it may start to be a little bit more asymmetric   for the for the 5-year yield part of the curve  where yields can move lower and start to hedge   some of the uh you know the exposure that  are in uh global investment portfolios.   Thanks, George, for your insights. Happy to have  you here. Great. Thanks very much. This episode of   Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Monday,  September 14th, 2026.
